item.title: Fresh Prep gets court approval to buy fellow meal kit company Goodfood
item.description: Canadian meal delivery company Fresh Prep Foods Inc. says it has received court permission to acquire distressed competitor Goodfood Market Corp.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Canadian meal delivery company Fresh Prep Foods Inc. says it has received court permission to acquire distressed competitor Goodfood Market Corp. Fresh Prep refused to disclose how much it will pay for Goodfood but says the deal is expected to close on or around Friday. Once the deal closes, Fresh Prep says it will begin serving about 30,000 Goodfood customers. Goodfood filed for creditor protection with the Superior Court of Quebec over the summer in hopes of restructuring under a new owner or with help from investors. The Montreal-based company started in 2014 and is known for selling pre-measured sets of ingredients and recipes to customers who cook them into meals. Fresh Prep operates similarly. It was founded in Vancouver in 2015 and acquired another Montreal-based meal kit company called Cook It Recipes Inc. in 2024. --- Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

item.title: Bank of Canada moving carefully, but further hikes might be needed: meeting summary
item.description: The Bank of Canada’s governing council thinks it might need to raise interest rates further, but it’s proceeding carefully, according to a summary of deliberations.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — The Bank of Canada’s governing council thinks it might need to raise interest rates further, but it’s proceeding carefully, according to a summary of deliberations of its recent decision to raise its key policy rate for the first time since 2023. According to the report, the council acknowledged it faced considerable uncertainty and said it would take its monetary policy decisions one meeting at a time. The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month to reduce the risk that stubbornly high oil prices become persistent inflation. The summary says the council members agreed that monetary policy cannot lower global energy prices, but can prevent them from leading to generalized inflation. The decision came as the Bank of Canada raised its outlook for the annual inflation rate to hit 3.5 per cent at the end of this year and remain above three per cent for much of 2027. The summary of deliberations said higher costs largely haven’t been passed through to consumers so far, but the bank’s surveys suggest businesses expect to raise some prices over the next year. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

item.title: World shares rise after technology shares advance on Wall Street ahead of U.S. inflation data
item.description: Global markets were higher Tuesday after U.S. stocks rallied, recovering most of their big losses from last week, while investors awaited U.S. inflation data for October.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — U.S. stocks are falling Tuesday after a report showed inflation was worse across the country last month than economists expected. The S&P 500 fell 0.9 per cent and gave back some of its big rally from the day before. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 319 points, or 0.6 per cent, as of 1:29 p.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.4 per cent lower. Pressure from the bond market undercut stocks following the discouraging report on inflation. People had to pay prices for groceries, electricity and other costs of living that were even higher last month than economists expected. That could push the Federal Reserve to hike its main interest rate at its next meeting in December and beyond. Higher interest rates can help rein in inflation, but they do so by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money and by slowing the overall economy. Higher rates also make investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other investments. One Fed official even hinted the central bank may increase the federal funds rate by double the typical amount next month because of how high inflation has remained for years. Speaking in London before the inflation report was released, Fed Gov. Christopher Waller said “a stronger policy move may be needed” if the report showed an important underlying measure of inflation rose by 0.3 per cent from September. In that case, he said the Fed should consider hiking the federal funds rate by half a percentage point rather than the typical quarter point. Moving by only the usual amount could “put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.” Shortly afterward, Tuesday’s inflation report showed that the underlying measure of inflation Waller was worried about was exactly 0.3 per cent, the threshold he had set. It’s the Fed’s job to keep inflation under control, along with keeping the job market strong. That sent yields jumping in the bond market as traders upped their forecasts for coming hikes to rates by the Fed. The yield on the 10-year Treasury jumped to 5.01 per cent from 4.88 per cent late Monday. It’s a notable move for the bond market, and the yield helps set where rates are for mortgages and other loans going to U.S. households and businesses. The 10-year Treasury yield had been dropping since early October, when it topped 5.30 per cent as worries spiked about high inflation, higher interest rates, the U.S. government’s big debt and other concerns. Tuesday’s jump in yields came even though oil prices fell again. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 0.8 per cent to US$91.81. U.S. President Donald Trump said late Monday that the war in Iran, which sent oil prices much higher, “militarily is effectively over.” Brent’s price has been falling from more than US$112 at the start of the month amid uncertainty about what will happen with the war with Iran. Jumps in Treasury yields push downward on prices for all kinds of stocks, and they can particularly hurt companies in the real-estate business. Higher mortgage rates can keep potential customers away from homebuilders, for example, and Lennar fell 4.4 per cent for one of the sharper losses in the S&P 500. Rival homebuilders also fell, including drops of 3.6 per cent for D.R. Horton and 3.5 per cent for PulteGroup. Builders FirstSource, which sells crown mouldings, cabinets and other products to homebuilders, sank 3.9 per cent. The single heaviest weight on the S&P 500 was Nvidia, which fell 6.3 per cent. It’s been under pressure since its board announced an investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, who admitted to a relationship with a woman who, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for China. It’s also been swinging amid broader worries that have knocked the artificial-intelligence industry around recently. Democratic victories in statehouses across the country last week raised concerns about possible restrictions on construction of AI data centres. That built on top of already longstanding worries that AI stock prices had shot too high and were in a bubble. Other stocks in the AI industry also slipped. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, dropped 7 per cent. Micron Technology, which sells memory for computers, fell 3.6 per cent after flipping between gains and losses earlier in the morning. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 2.6 per cent. Advanced Micro Devices held up better and was mostly unchanged. The recent shakiness for AI-related stocks had raised questions about whether Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, may delay its initial public offering of stock. But Anthropic said in a filing with U.S. regulators on Tuesday that it’s looking to sell its stock at a price valuing the company at roughly US$1.3 trillion. That would make it one of the most valuable companies on Wall Street, worth more than Walmart, JPMorgan Chase, ExxonMobil or Coca-Cola. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 4.4 per cent for one of the world’s biggest gains on strength for its two tech giants that have benefited from the AI boom, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Writers Elaine Lai and Matt Ott contributed to this report.

item.title: Christine Poole’s Top Picks for Nov. 10, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Christine Poole, President & Co-Chief Investment Officer, Davis Rea Focus: North American Large Caps

Top Picks: Microsoft , RTX Corp , Stryker MARKET OUTLOOK: In October, the contrast in performance between the headline S&P 500 Index and the S&P 500 Equal Weight Index highlighted a significant broadening in market breadth. The market cap weighted index was down 0.9 per cent in the month while the equal weighted index was up 4.9 per cent. Broadening market breadth means the participation in a stock market rally is expanding beyond a concentrated handful of mega-cap technology companies to include a wider variety of companies across diverse sectors. The Democratic sweep in the midterm elections has added uncertainty to the pace of the AI buildout and put additional downward pressure on AI-related stocks. The resilient U.S. economy continues to expand, supported by strength in consumer spending and private business AI-related investment. U.S GDP grew by 2.2 per cent in the second quarter and accelerated to 3.4 per cent in the third quarter. The unemployment rate is low, hovering around four per cent. Leading economic indicators reinforce durable momentum with the ISM Manufacturing Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) signaling expansion for ten consecutive months, and the Services PMI expanding for 28 consecutive months. However, inflation continues to be stubbornly above the Federal Reserve’s long-term two per cent target, serving as the primary reason for the central bank’s September rate hike. The Canadian economy is expanding at a more modest pace, anchored by subdued consumer spending, muted population growth, and ongoing trade-related pressures. According to the Bank of Canada’s latest Monetary Policy report, GDP is expected to be two per cent in the third quarter and slow to below one per cent in the fourth quarter. The unemployment rate has been around 6.5 per cent, pointing to excess supply in the economy. While core inflation (excluding gasoline) remains close to two per cent, the Bank of Canada increased interest rates in October as a preventative measure in anticipation of increased cost pass-through as higher energy prices and tariff-related costs are eventually priced into consumer goods and services. Looking ahead to next year, economic growth in Canada is projected to improve due to stronger business investment, bolstered by federal tax incentives such as the Productivity Mega Deduction, and government spending. The long-term sustainability of spending in AI and continued growth in consumer spending, which accounts for about 70 per cent of U.S. GDP, are key drivers for continued U.S. economic prosperity. A caveat to a slower pace of AI investment is reduced inflationary pressures for technology goods. Our investment framework shifts away from market timing and toward what we can control: owning reasonably priced, high-quality companies within industries that offer attractive secular growth or stable income generation. Staying invested in a diversified portfolio with an asset mix geared to your risk tolerance and financial capacity is the path to preserving and generating long-term wealth. How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google Market-moving news, fast:  Get the BNN Bloomberg App now Sign up for the Market Call Top Picks newsletter at  bnnbloomberg.ca/newsletters TOP PICKS: Christine Poole’s Top Picks: Microsoft, RTX Corp & Stryker Christine Poole, president & co-chief investment officer at Davis Rea, shares her top stock picks to watch in the market.

Microsoft (MSFT NASD) Microsoft is a global technology company providing a wide range of software services and products including Windows, Office 365, LinkedIn, and Azure cloud computing as well as owning a leading gaming platform, Xbox, and video game publisher, Activision Blizzard. Its growing recurring revenue, robust cloud computing growth, and strong balance sheet are appealing investment attributes. Microsoft’s dividend yield is 0.7 per cent. RTX Corp (RTX NYSE) RTX is a aerospace and defense company engaged in providing advanced systems and services for commercial, military and government customers. Its product portfolio includes avionics, interiors, aircraft engines, sensor and communication systems and missile defense systems. Its commercial aerospace businesses benefit from the growth in global air travel while demand for its defense products is robust due to ongoing geopolitical conflicts. The stock provides a dividend yield of 1.5 per cent. Stryker (SYK NYSE) Stryker is a leading medical technology company offering a broad portfolio of products and services across neurotechnology and orthopedics, including knee and hip implants, surgical equipment, and neurovascular devices. Approximately 75 per cent of the company’s revenue is generated in the United States, with the remaining 25 per cent derived from international markets. Stryker is estimated to hold 75 per cent of the U.S. orthopedic surgical robotics market, providing a strong competitive position. Stryker is also well positioned to benefit from demographic trends, particularly an aging population and the associated increase in demand for joint replacements and surgical procedures. Stryker has a track record of dividend growth and offers a dividend yield of one per cent.
